Two graphs over the same project, answering two different questions.

| | map | product diagram |
|---|---|---|
| node | a claim | a part of the built thing |
| question | why is it like this | what is there now |
| shape | history, append-only | current state, overwritten |
| goes stale | by propagation | the moment code lands |

The map already answers why. Nothing renders what. The set of decided cards implies a system — UI, agent, log, fold, CLI, server — and today that system exists only in the reader's head.

Corrected from the earlier version of this card, which claimed the product diagram was just a new node kind inside the map. It is not. The prototype's result is not "hand-drawn SVG is better". It is **the agent chose the lanes and the order well, and did the arithmetic badly**. In `.werk/diagram-a.svg` it computed 22 label plates as `chars * 5.6 + 8` by hand. Split on that line.

About 300 lines for the resolver, 120 for the checker — one afternoon.
2. **Same, plus a skill file for taste only** — what belongs in which lane, what the seven colours mean, when to split a group. No numbers in the markdown. This is the combination you asked about, and it is option 1 with the prompt half written down.
3. **Custom Mermaid renderer** — rejected. The failure was auto-layout, not rendering, and Mermaid's syntax cannot carry lane or order.
4. **Constrained auto-layout (ELK)** — rejected. It takes the placement choice back from the agent, which is the one thing that worked.

One fact makes this cheap: werk draws its own picture in a browser, so the resolver can call `measureText`. Exact text width, no font table, no estimate.

## How grid diagrams work in D2D2's grid diagram layout arranges objects in row and column structures. Grid diagrams are a specialized layout mode that positions child objects in a structured grid pattern, distinct from the default graph-based layouts provided by Dagre and ELK. This layout is triggered when an object has `grid-rows` or `grid-columns` attributes set.

From the Go package docs: Layout runs the grid layout on containers with rows/columns — note that children are not allowed edges or descendants.

## Key behaviors

**Dominant direction:** The dominant direction is the order in which cells are filled. Since `grid-rows` is defined first, objects will fill rows before moving onto columns — declaring `grid-columns` first reverses this.

**Cell sizing:** Elements in a grid column have the same width and elements in a grid row have the same height. This can produce unexpected empty space when one label is longer than its neighbors.

**Alignment trick:** To center content, you can add invisible elements as padding.

**Nesting:** The layout process operates on the graph root's immediate children, arranging them into a grid structure. Children of grid cells may themselves be nested grids, allowing recursive grid layouts.

**Auto-balancing:** When only rows OR columns are specified, D2 optimizes the distribution to balance total dimensions via a `getBestLayout` search function.

## Basic syntax

```d2
grid_container: {
  grid-rows: 2
  grid-columns: 3
  item1; item2; item3
  item4; item5; item6
}
```This pattern comes from a D2 skill reference showing grid usage for structured layouts.

Related attributes seen in real-world examples include `grid-gap`, `horizontal-gap`, and `vertical-gap` — for instance, a container using `grid-columns: 1`, `horizontal-gap: 24`, and `vertical-gap: 20` to stack layered architecture sections, with an inner `grid-rows: 4` / `grid-gap: 22` block.

## Useful links

- **Official docs:** https://d2lang.com/tour/grid-diagrams/
- **Implementation deep-dive:** https://deepwiki.com/terrastruct/d2/3.3-grid-diagram-layout
- **Go package:** https://pkg.go.dev/oss.terrastruct.com/d2/d2layouts/d2grid
- **Real example (architecture diagram):** https://blog.jread.com/posts/d2-is-a-great-language-for-architecture-diagrams/

One gotcha worth noting: since grid children can't have connections *to* each other in the traditional sense in older versions, check the docs section on grid connections if you need edges between cells.

## libavoid (part of Adaptagrams)

**What it is:** libavoid is a cross-platform C++ library providing fast, object-avoiding orthogonal and polyline connector routing for use in interactive diagram editors, and is part of the Adaptagrams project. It is written and maintained by Michael Wybrow of the Immersive Analytics Lab at Monash University, Australia.

**The broader project:** The Adaptagrams libraries are collectively known as cola (for Constraint Layout), and the code is written by Tim Dwyer, Michael Wybrow and Steve Kieffer of the Immersive Analytics Lab at Monash University. Other components include libtopology (extensions to libcola for topology-preserving constraint-based layout) and libdialect (for computing human-like orthogonal network layouts).

**Licensing:** libavoid is available under the GNU Lesser General Public License v2.1, with commercial licenses also available by contacting Michael Wybrow.

## The Wybrow–Marriott–Stuckey papers

Two key papers underpin the routing algorithms:

1. Wybrow, Marriott, and Stuckey, "Incremental connector routing," in Proceedings of the 13th International Symposium on Graph Drawing, LNCS 3843, pages 446–457, Springer-Verlag, 2006.

2. **"Orthogonal Connector Routing"** (GD 2009) — by Michael Wybrow, Kim Marriott, and Peter J. Stuckey. The abstract notes that most interactive diagram editors use ad-hoc heuristics that can produce strange routes or routes passing through objects; the authors present an algorithm for computing optimal object-avoiding orthogonal connector routings that minimizes a monotonic function of connector length and number of bends, fast enough to reroute during interaction.

**Algorithm structure:** The paper shows a three-step process analogous to polyline routing can be used for optimal orthogonal routing: an *orthogonal visibility graph* whose edges represent horizontal/vertical lines of visibility from vertices and connector ports of each object; routes found via A* search through that graph; with a guarantee of optimality in minimizing bends and overall connector length. The three stages are: (a) the orthogonal visibility graph, (b) optimal connector routes, and (c) final routes after centering and nudging — the third stage computing the visual representation of the connector. The algorithm finds an optimal valid route for a single connector through the orthogonal visibility graph in O(n² log n) time.

**Penrose** is a system developed at Carnegie Mellon University for automatically generating mathematical diagrams from high-level notation. It was developed by Wode Ni, Katherine Ye, Joshua Sunshine, Jonathan Aldrich, and Keenan Crane, as a system to automatically visualize mathematics from notation.

## MotivationFormalizing diagrams in most general-purpose tools requires painstaking low-level manipulation of shapes and positions. Unlike low-level tools such as Adobe Illustrator, where diagrams are specified via graphical primitives, a mathematically-inclined user should not require graphic design skill to create beautiful diagrams. A general-purpose tool like TikZ has no notion of the domain a user is illustrating, so it exposes total control over display attributes — making it difficult to illustrate multiple objects without duplicating code, or to cleanly illustrate an object in different ways.

## The Three LanguagesPenrose features three languages: *Substance* for specifying the content of a diagram, *Domain* for defining the content primitives, and *Style* for visualizing the Substance specification.

**Domain** — defines the vocabulary of a subject area. For example, the simplest Domain schema describing a directed graph declares a `Vertex` type and an `Arc(Vertex a, Vertex b)` predicate.

**Substance** — tells Penrose what objects and relations to draw. Notably, it contains no instructions about how a `Set` must be rendered; it only declares the existence of objects and relations. It is a declarative language that resembles standard mathematical notation.

A Style program is composed of three block types: namespaces (for constants like canvas dimensions and colors), selector blocks (which match on Substance statements), and collector blocks (which aggregate match results into collections). Selectors use pattern matching rather than literal string matching — the `forall` keyword matches every instance of a type.

## The core distinction

Structurizr is a "models as code" tool designed for the C4 model — you write Structurizr DSL to create multiple software architecture diagrams from a single model. It was created by the author of the C4 model and remains the reference implementation. It is not a traditional drag-and-drop UI tool and does not provide a way to make diagrams via a UI; instead you write DSL and Structurizr renders the diagrams.

## Manual layout is supported (unlike most diagrams-as-code tools)

Simon Brown addresses a common misconception directly: a false narrative exists that UI-driven tools support manual layout while "as code" tools don't — it is true that most diagrams-as-code formats (PlantUML, Mermaid, dot, etc.) only support automatic layout. Structurizr is relatively unique in supporting both automatic and manual layout via a browser-based diagram editor, enabling more precise storytelling.

## How layout data is stored

This is the key practical detail: although Structurizr is a "models as code" tool, diagram layout information generally isn't something you author by hand — element x,y positions are not stored in your DSL workspace definition, but in a JSON version of the workspace (schema published on GitHub).

The rationale for manual layout: when authoring your workspace you choose automatic or manual layout, and architecture diagrams are storytelling tools, often more effective when manual layout precisely positions elements.

## Gotchas with manual layout

Layout can be lost when the DSL changes: changing the order of lines in the DSL can mean an element can't be matched and its layout information is lost, while entire diagrams losing layout is generally caused by changing a view's key — to minimise this, use explicit keys for views rather than letting the DSL parser generate them.

## Auto layout

For auto layout you simply add `autoLayout` inside a view block, as in Brown's introductory example. By default Structurizr doesn't focus heavily on layout because with Structurizr online or Structurizr Lite you can adjust diagrams manually and positions are recorded. There are third-party workarounds for hybrid control — one project aims to use auto-layout while having a bit more control over it, via view `properties` such as a direction hint between two containers to control which side a relationship exits from when exporting to C4-PlantUML.

**Practical takeaway:** use `autoLayout` for fast-moving or generated diagrams and diagrams rendered through PlantUML/Mermaid exporters; use manual layout (via Lite/cloud editor, persisted in workspace JSON committed alongside your DSL) for high-visibility diagrams where the narrative matters — and always set explicit view keys so that layout survives refactoring.

## The foundational work

**"Validating Graph Drawing Aesthetics" (Purchase, Cohen & James)**Designers of graph drawing algorithms and systems claim to illuminate application data by producing layouts that optimize measurable aesthetic qualities. Examples of these aesthetics include symmetry, minimizing edge crossings, and minimizing bends. The aim of this paper is to describe our work to validate these claims by performing empirical studies of human understanding of graphs drawn using various layout aesthetics. The authors note there had been very little work in this area, and that this was the first study to address the effect of aesthetics on general understanding of graphs, with prior work having focused on specific applications and 2D/3D comparisons. This user study examined the effects of five graph drawing aesthetics (including symmetry, edge crossings, angular resolution, and orthogonality) on task performance. ## The `-n` flag

The `-n[num]` flag sets the no-op flag in neato. If set, neato assumes nodes have already been positioned and all nodes have a `pos` attribute giving the positions. It then performs an optional adjustment to remove node-node overlap (depending on the `overlap` attribute), computes the edge layouts (depending on the `splines` attribute), and emits the graph in the appropriate format.

**Variants:**
- `-n` / `-n1` — equivalent to each other; positions used, but overlap removal and edge routing still happen.
- `-n2` — uses node positions as specified with no adjustment to remove node-node overlaps, and uses any edge layouts already specified by the `pos` attribute. neato computes an edge layout for any edge that does not have a `pos` attribute, guided as usual by the `splines` attribute.

## Units gotcha

This is the most common source of confusion: by default, fdp and neato interpret the x and y values of `pos` as being in inches, but `neato -n(2)` treats the coordinates as being in points — the unit used by the layout algorithms for the `pos` attribute. So if your graph has `pos` attributes in points, you should set `inputscale=72`.Because the `-n` flag assumes positions were set by one of the layout programs (and are therefore in points), `neato -n` accepts input correctly without requiring a `-s` flag and in fact ignores any such flag.

## Typical invocation

The Graphviz FAQ addresses exactly this case — if you already have all the coordinates for the nodes and edges and just want to render it, put the graph with layout attributes into a dot file, then run something like `neato -s -nop -Tgif file.dot -o file.gif`. In modern usage you'd typically just write:

```
neato -n2 -Tsvg graph.dot -o graph.svg
```

## Alternative: `pin` / `!` suffix

If you'd rather keep the layout engine running but freeze certain nodes, use pinning instead: if `pin=true` and the node has a `pos` attribute on input, neato or fdp prevents the node from moving from the input position. This property can also be specified in the `pos` attribute itself (the trailing `!` on the point value). Note that `pos` is honored for layout purposes by neato and fdp only — running `dot` will ignore it entirely.

A known pitfall reported by users: writing `pos="10,10!"` with `pin=true` alone may not produce output that uses those coordinates except in the canon format, which is precisely why passing `-n`/`-n2` is the reliable approach.

**Sources:** [Graphviz `pos` docs](https://graphviz.org/docs/attrs/pos/) · [Graphviz Attributes](https://graphviz.org/doc/info/attrs.html) · [Command-line Invocation](https://web.mit.edu/spin_v4.2.5/share/graphviz/doc/html/info/command.html)

**Important update: TALA is no longer proprietary.**

**Current status (as of September 2026)**TALA (Terrastruct Automatic Layout Algorithm) is now open-source under the MPL-2.0 license. The source code is hosted in the d2lang/d2 repository on GitHub, and it is bundled by default with version 0.9.0 and later of D2, usable by specifying `--layout=tala` on the command line. The announcement drew significant attention, reaching 235 points on Hacker News.

The D2 repo now describes it as a bundled, opt-in native layout and edge-routing engine designed specifically for software architecture diagrams, selectable via `--layout=tala`, `D2_LAYOUT=tala`, or a `layout-engine: tala` setting under `vars.d2-config`.

**The old proprietary model (now outdated)**

Docs and pages that haven't been updated still reflect the former licensing:

- It was described as a proprietary layout engine developed by Terrastruct, installed separately from D2 to keep a clean cut between 100% free and open-source D2 and proprietary, closed-source TALA.
- It was a paid layout engine requiring a license for any commercial use, purchasable from Terrastruct.
- **Free tier / evaluation:** TALA was freely installable and locally runnable for evaluation, requiring an API token from a Terrastruct account to run out of evaluation mode, and without a license it rendered with a watermark.
- **License types:** Personal and Enterprise — Enterprise licenses allowed running TALA on servers such as CI/CD environments, Personal licenses were for individual desktop/machine usage, and diagrams made on a Personal license belonged to the creator.
- Those licenses only applied to D2 Studio and TALA; D2 itself has always been FOSS under the Mozilla Public License 2.0.

**Bottom line:** If you're on D2 0.9.0+, you get TALA bundled under MPL-2.0 with no license key, token, or watermark. Any guidance you find about purchasing a TALA license or evaluation watermarks predates the September 2026 open-sourcing.

Here's what I found about `@terrastruct/d2` (D2.js):

## OverviewD2.js is a JavaScript wrapper around D2, the modern diagram scripting language. It enables running D2 directly in browsers and Node environments through WebAssembly. It works in both browser and Node environments, and is built with ESM modules with a CJS fallback.

## Installation

```bash
npm install @terrastruct/d2
# or: yarn add / pnpm add / bun add
```
You can also use the `@nightly` tag to get the version built by daily CI on the master branch.

## Basic usage
The same code works for Node or browser:

```js
import { D2 } from '@terrastruct/d2';
// Or using a CDN:
// import { D2 } from 'https://esm.sh/@terrastruct/d2';

const d2 = new D2();
const result = await d2.compile('x -> y');
const svg = await d2.render(result.diagram, result.renderOptions);
```

The API surface is small: `new D2()` creates an instance, `compile()` compiles D2 markup into an intermediate representation, and `render()` renders a compiled diagram to SVG.

## Virtual filesystem / importsYou can pass a `fs` object with multiple files plus an `inputPath` and options (e.g. `sketch: true`) to `compile()`, which supports `@import` between files.

```js
const fs = {
  "project.d2": "a: @import",
  "import.d2": "x: {shape: circle}",
};
const result = await d2.compile({ fs, inputPath: "project.d2", options: { sketch: true } });
```

## Implementation notes
- D2.js uses web workers to call a WASM file. This matters for bundler configuration (worker + `.wasm` asset handling).
- It is essentially a wrapper around the WASM build of D2, and is available via CDNs like jsDelivr and esm.sh.
- Building from source: clone the repo, then run `./make.sh all` in `d2/d2js/js`; binaryen is recommended for optimal WASM file size, and the local example page runs at `http://localhost:3000`. The build toolchain uses Bun.

## Related
- Go library usage (server-side rendering) is documented in the main repo's `docs/examples/lib`, where there are examples showing how to use the D2 library to turn D2 scripts into rendered SVG diagrams.
- D2 itself supports SVG, PNG, and PDF exports, though the JS/WASM path centers on SVG output.

Here's what I found on D2's text measurement and font embedding:

## D2's `d2/lib/textmeasure` package

The package exposes a `Ruler` type plus markdown measurement functions such as `MeasureMarkdown(mdText string, ruler *Ruler, fontFamily *d2fonts.FontFamily, monoFontFamily *d2fonts.FontFamily, fontSize int) (width, height int, err error)`, and `NewAtlas(face font.Face, runeSets ...[]rune)`, which creates an atlas containing glyphs.

For markdown labels, D2 hardcodes a set of layout constants — including `MarkdownFontSize`, `MarkdownLineHeight = 1.5`, and margin/padding values like `MarginBottom_p = 16`, `LineHeight_h = 1.25`, `LineHeight_pre = 1.45` — described as CSS values taken from github-markdown.css so the rendered dimensions can be accurately computed.

## Embedded fonts and deterministic output

This is the key part for your question. From the `d2renderers/d2fonts` docs: the SVG renderer embeds fonts directly into the SVG as base64 data, in order to give deterministic outputs and load without a network call; to include your own font (e.g. Helvetica) you must supply the TrueType glyphs.

Since layout dimensions are computed server-side from the embedded font's metrics rather than from a browser's `getBBox()`, the measured box and the rendered text agree regardless of what fonts the viewer has installed.

## Size optimization

Embedding whole fonts was costly, so D2 subsets them. As of 0.3.0, SVG sizes are about 5% of what they were in D2 0.2 — the font was the largest contributor, and D2 now bundles only the used portion (if you don't use the letter "b", its font encoding isn't included). That release also added customizable fonts passable via command-line flags.

## Related context

A comparable Go package for Mermaid-style diagrams describes the same motivation: it computes text bounding boxes from font metrics as a replacement for the browser's `SVGTextElement.getBBox()`, because layout needs accurate text dimensions to size nodes — a 10% width error cascades into overlapping labels. Its `Measure` returns pixel width/height at a given font size, with multi-line text returning max line width and summed line heights.

Useful links: [pkg.go.dev/oss.terrastruct.com/d2/lib/textmeasure](https://pkg.go.dev/oss.terrastruct.com/d2/lib/textmeasure) and the [d2fonts source](https://github.com/d2lang/d2/tree/master/d2renderers/d2fonts).

## The core package: `libavoid-js`

It's a JS port of the libavoid library, currently at version 0.5.0-beta.5 on npm. Libavoid itself is a C++ library offering high-quality polyline and orthogonal link routing that navigates around objects and avoids overlapping parallel links — libavoid-js is its JavaScript port.

**Build details:** The port is generated via Emscripten + WebIDL bindings. WebIDL is powerful, but the emscripten implementation isn't very actively developed — if a feature like callback support is missing or you hit a bug, expect to fix it yourself. Building requires Git (to clone the original libavoid library and build tools) and generates both release and debug versions plus updated docs.

**Common gotcha:** A frequent FAQ issue is an invalid `libavoid.wasm`. The advice is to check the browser's Network tab to confirm it downloaded without errors and matches the expected file size.

**Performance:** A bachelor's thesis on the subject notes that measurements show libavoid-js is 8–11 times slower than native libavoid — a large difference, but sufficient for many small and medium use cases.

|---|---|
| `@mr_mint/elkjs-libavoid` | Obstacle-avoiding edge routing for ELK JSON graphs using libavoid (TypeScript, v0.5.0) |
| `avoid-nodes-edge` | Orthogonal edge routing for React Flow — edges avoid overlapping nodes via libavoid-js WASM running in a Web Worker |

| `sprotty-routing-libavoid` | Sprotty integration; configured via `router.setOptions({ routingType: RouteType.Orthogonal, segmentPenalty, idealNudgingDistance, shapeBufferDistance, ... })` |

Two things decide this, and neither is settled:

1. **The equal-cell rule.** A D2 grid column forces one width on every member, and a row forces one height. That is how Mermaid produced the empty regions Eryk rejected in #vi-sysdiag-svg. node src/cli.ts edit vi-sysdiag-lint --body 'The checker reads the intent file and the resolved geometry, and reports, as text the agent can act on:

1. Two boxes overlap, or a box overlaps a lane frame.
2. Text is wider than its box, or a label plate is wider than its edge run.
3. An edge crosses another edge, or passes through a box it does not connect.
4. An edge has no label, or a node has no card id.
5. Anything is outside the viewBox.

The agent redraws until the checker is silent. Eryk sees only the clean result.

Rules 1, 2 and 5 are errors: the resolver should make them impossible, so one firing is a resolver bug. Rule 4 catches a fold that dropped content, which is the failure #vi-sysdiag-proto is actually testing for.

Rule 3 was going to be a warning. #purchase-aesthetics says otherwise: of five aesthetics tested, edge crossings hurt comprehension by far the most, with bends second. So the crossing count is the main number the checker reports, and the agent is expected to act on it. Ware et al. refine it further — the crossings that cost the reader are the ones on the path the reader follows — so the count is reported per edge, not only as a total.

See #vi-sysdiag-render for the split this sits inside.'

Ten source cards are on the map, linked to the four cards they support. One finding changes the plan.

**#vi-sysdiag-d2 — buy the resolver, do not write it.** D2's `grid-rows` / `grid-columns` takes placement from the author, not from a solver — the one property that made your SVG read well. TALA, the engine that actually *routes* edges instead of drawing centre-to-centre lines, went MPL-2.0 on 2026-09-08 and now ships inside D2 0.9.0. Four days ago this option did not exist. It covers all seven passes, and `@terrastruct/d2` runs as WASM in Node and the browser.

Two risks, both on the card: a D2 grid column forces one width on every member, which is how Mermaid made the empty regions you rejected; and werk gains its first dependency.

Component mapping from the research:

| piece | prior art |
|---|---|
| intent holds no numbers | #penrose — Substance has no numeric type at all |
| ids must survive a redraw | #structurizr — reordering DSL lines loses an element's layout |
| place, then render | #graphviz-nop — `neato -n2`, supported since the 1990s |
| exact text width | #d2-fonts and #satori — both embed the font and measure it, never `getBBox` |
| edge routing | #libavoid — optimal, not heuristic, with a WASM port |
| what the checker ranks | #purchase-aesthetics — crossings hurt comprehension most, so #vi-sysdiag-lint now treats rule 3 as the main number, not a warning |

Next: I write `.werk/diagram-a.svg` as D2 with `grid-rows`, render it with `--layout=tala`, and put it beside the hand SVG. One hour, and it settles the equal-width risk with a picture.

**What worked.** Text measurement is exact, every box fits its label, and no label overflows. The order declared with `grid-rows` inside MAP VIEW, CHAT PANE and STORE came out exactly as written. Edge colour classes work. The intent half of #vi-sysdiag-intent survives the translation with almost no loss.

**A, full root grid.** Every top-level container gets the width of the widest one, so `cli`, `claude code child` and `issue tracker` each stretch to 1500 px for a two-line label. 3517 x 2210, against 1800 x 1380 by hand.

**B, grid inside containers, TALA places the top level.** Compact, and the closest to the hand drawing in density. It also overlaps: the STORE frame sits on top of the SERVER PROCESS frame, and three nodes are drawn over the CHAT PANE frame. A solver chose the top-level positions and chose wrong.

**C, root grid with the three loose nodes wrapped in an invisible row.** No overlap, right structure, and the failure is the one Eryk already rejected: the SERVER PROCESS and STORE frames are full width because BROWSER is, so the right half of each is empty. 3536 x 1734, aspect 2.04 against 1.30 by hand. Cross-container edges — "reads every past decision", "runs the agent", "saves the conversation" — route around the outside of the whole canvas instead of through the empty middle.

**The finding.** A D2 grid gives order, not proportion. A column is one width and a row is one height for every member, and there is no column span. The hand drawing reads well partly because the widths are unequal: `http + sse` spans the full server, `cli` is small. That is not expressible, and the documented workaround is invisible spacers, which is hand-tuning under a new name — variants A and C already needed three of them.

So D2 does not replace #vi-sysdiag-resolve. It does settle #vi-sysdiag-metrics: #d2-fonts is the proof that subset-the-font-into-the-SVG works, in a shipping tool.

Open, because rejecting it is Eryk''s call, not mine. Untried levers: `near` for shape-relative placement, explicit `width` and `height` on containers, and `grid-gap`.'

card werk-hmr  [decided]
Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
why: Settled by research, two rounds of real-app testing, a direct repro of the one open correctness concern, and Eryk's own priorities on productionization and upgrade risk. See #werk-hmr:src0 through src5, and options opt1/opt2.

The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees globalThis survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Toy prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): a minimal Agent-shaped harness, globalThis-pinned, survived edits to both a sibling module and the pinned module itself, under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch.

Real-app test, unpatched (#werk-hmr:src2): werk's real code has neither guard. vite-node --watch crashed outright on an unrelated-file edit (EADDRINUSE retry loop, process.exit(1)). bun --hot did not crash, but silently orphaned a live task on the same edit.

Fix, real-app test, patched (#werk-hmr:src3): one guard clause in server.ts's serve() (globalThis.__werkServe check) fixed both candidates identically. Both now survive a real in-flight task through a src edit, verified with a fresh-connection check. Side effect worth knowing: this guard also means a hot reload stops applying code changes inside serve()'s body - the tradeoff is 'my live session survives an edit' over 'my latest route-handler edit is live', which is correct for the original problem.

Runtime research (#werk-hmr:src4, Sept 2026): general research flagged one concrete objection to Bun as werk's runtime - oven-sh/bun #7716/#13811, open issues about SSE 'close' not firing reliably on client disconnect, which sounded like it hit werk's server.ts directly.

Direct repro (#werk-hmr:src5): tested against Bun 1.4.1 specifically (the exact version used throughout, and the one the research flagged as the big Zig-to-Rust rewrite). Added a probe to werk's actual /api/live handler and disconnected SSE clients both cleanly and via kill -9. close fired correctly every time, clients.delete(res) ran, no leak. The bug is real and filed, but does not reproduce for werk's specific pattern.

Decided: move werk's runtime to Bun (bun --hot). The one concrete correctness objection did not reproduce on werk's own code on the exact version tested (1.4.1). The remaining Bun tradeoffs are a values call, not a correctness one, and Eryk's priorities resolve them: bun build --compile is a real asset for productionizing werk as a shipped tool (Node's own SEA docs mark it 'Stability: 1.1 - Active development', a weaker position), and Bun's faster breaking-change cadence is an acceptable cost given agents do the upgrade work rather than a single unaided maintainer. #werk-hmr:opt2 records staying on Node as the rejected alternative; #werk-hmr:opt1 records the original Bun rejection, superseded once #werk-hmr:src5 tested it directly.

Please check in Network tab of the browser, that it is downloaded without errors and its size is the same as of [libavoid.wasm file](https://github.com/Aksem/libavoid-js/blob/master/dist/libavoid.wasm). 26 27 ## Build 28 29 ### Requirements 30 31 - Git (to clone original libavoid library) 32 - Docker (used to run emcc) 33 - Python 3.5+ (used for tooling/build automation) 34 35 ### Build commands 36 37 1. `npm run full-rebuild` 38 39 It will generate both release and debug versions of the library, also update documentation. 40 41 2. If you want only to rebuild JS package without regenerating bindings, you can use the following command: `npm run build` 42 43 ### Debugging 44 45 Address to source map is hardcoded in `tools/generate.py` script and is always 'http://localhost:8080' in debug build. 46 47 Also, symlink to adaptagrams should be in `examples` directory to provide libavoid sources for debugger. 48 49 ## Lessons learned 50 51 - WebIDL is a powerful concept, but implementation in emscripten toolset is not very actively developed and if certain feature is missing such as support of callbacks or you encounter a bug, you should be ready to implement or to fix it by yourself. We started with WebIDL(own fork with implementation of callbacks, support of prefixed enums and more) and then switched to embind. Embind supports more features, so probability you need to modify it is lower, and it is more performant. 52 53 ## History 54 55 This project was started as part of a research project at [Technische Universität Wien](https://www.tuwien.at) and is further developed by its author and contributors. 56 57 58 59 60

48	  return { kind: 'row', items, w, h }

Four systemic finishing rules: card margin, label spacing, forced straight entry, label wrapping
why: Screenshots from the libavoid render showed four separate, recurring defects, not one-off glitches: a line grazing a card with no clearance, adjacent labels with no gap reading as one string, an edge entering a card sideways when it should always enter straight, and a long label pushing its neighbors out of position. Four rules, each mechanical, each independent of the others:

1. **Card margin.** Every line and label plate keeps a minimum clearance from every box it does not connect to.
2. **Label separation.** Two label plates that land near each other keep a minimum gap — currently 6px (LABEL_GAP), effectively invisible; raising it is the fix.
3. **Forced straight entry.** An edge assigned to a boxs top pin always makes its final approach vertical, arriving from above. Same for bottom (from below), left (from the right side... from further left), right (from further right). Never a sideways nudge into a top/bottom pin, never an up/down nudge into a side pin.
4. **Label wrapping.** A label wider than some cap wraps to multiple lines inside its plate, instead of one long plate that shoves its neighbors aside when decluttered.

Rule 3 is the one #vi-sysdiag-libavoid-pins already investigated and left unresolved — anglePenalty and two nudge options made no difference because both path shapes cost the router the same number of bends. The fix there is not a routing parameter. It is a geometric correction after the fact: insert a short perpendicular stub between the pin and whatever bend the router chose, so the segment touching the pin is always axis-correct, regardless of what libavoid returns.

## Handoff: system diagram renderer

**What this is.** A pipeline that turns a hand-authored intent file into an SVG system diagram, with real obstacle-avoiding edge routing and a mechanical checker. Lives under `src/sysdiag/`, ~1170 lines across 8 files. Not part of werk's own map/chat — it's a separate sub-project for rendering *this codebase's* architecture, currently the "Resolver + libavoid" tab in the Diagram view.

**Build and view it:**
```
bun src/sysdiag/build.ts .werk/diagram-a.intent .werk/diagram-a-libavoid.svg --router=libavoid
```
Reads `.werk/diagram-a.intent` (the source of truth — hand-edited, ~46 lines), writes the SVG, prints checker warnings/errors to stdout. Drop `--router=libavoid` to use the built-in router instead (`diagram-a-resolved.svg`) — kept only as a comparison baseline; it has no obstacle avoidance and will show 20 "runs through a box" errors on this intent file. Always use `--router=libavoid`.

To view: `werk serve` (or the running dev server), Diagram tab, **Resolver + libavoid** button. That button's wiring is in `src/server.ts` (`/api/diagram-svg?style=libavoid`) and `web/index.html`/`web/app.js` — those don't need touching for further geometry work, only if adding another named style.

**Pipeline, file by file:**
- `types.ts` — `IntentDoc`/`IntentNode`/`IntentGroup`/`IntentRow`/`IntentCols` (the authored AST), `Box`/`ResolvedEdge`/`Resolved` (the computed geometry).
- `parse.ts` — text → `IntentDoc`. Keywords: `group`, `cols` (side-by-side instead of stacked), `row`, `edge a -> b : <class> [@<card>] "<label>"`, `!fill` (a lone row stretches to its container's width).
- `metrics.ts` — real text measurement via a width table baked from headless Chrome's `canvas.measureText` (`.werk/font-metrics.json`), not an estimate. `wrapText()` does greedy word-wrap from real widths.
- `resolve.ts` — the core. `layoutDoc()` sizes and positions every box (bottom-up size pass, top-down position pass). `routeEdge()` is the built-in fallback router (one-bend orthogonal, no obstacle avoidance). `placeLabels()` places and declutters every edge's label. `finishDiagram()` computes the viewBox. All the tunable constants live at the top of this file (see below).
- `route-libavoid.ts` — the real router. Wraps `libavoid-js` (an actual npm dependency now — werk otherwise has zero). Also owns `straightenEnd()`, the polyline post-processor for forced-straight-entry (see below).
- `check.ts` — 7 mechanical rules, run after every build, printed as errors (must be zero) or warnings.
- `render.ts` — geometry → SVG string. No decisions made here.
- `build.ts` — CLI glue: parse → resolve/route → check → render → write.

**Current tunable constants** (`resolve.ts` unless noted):
```
BOX_CLEARANCE = 14        // min clearance, shared with route-libavoid's shapeBufferDistance
LABEL_GAP = 22            // min gap between adjacent label plates
MAX_LABEL_W = 130         // labels wider than this wrap
LABEL_LINE_H = 12
ROW_VGAP = 44             // vertical gap between sibling rows in a group
ROW_GAP = 18              // horizontal gap between nodes in a row
COLS_GAP = 32             // gap between side-by-side groups (cols)
```
`route-libavoid.ts`:
```
SPREAD = [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]  // 3 pins per side per box, not 1 — avoids one shared corridor
STUB = 16                 // straightenEnd's perpendicular-stub length, in px
anglePenalty = 200        // set explicitly; segmentPenalty = 50
```

**The 7 checker rules** (`check.ts`): 1 box-overlap, 2 text-overflows-its-own-box, 3 edge-crossings-and-runs-through-a-box, 4 missing-label/missing-card-id, 5 out-of-viewBox, 6 line-within-BOX_CLEARANCE-of-an-unrelated-box (warning), 7 label-plate-overlaps-a-box-including-its-own-endpoints (warning). Rules 1/2/5 firing means a resolver bug — arithmetic should make them impossible. Rule 3 hard-errors on "runs through," warns on "crosses." 6 and 7 are warnings because the router is only *asked* for clearance, not forced to it.

**What's fixed and verified this session, in order:**
1. libavoid replaced the built-in router for real obstacle avoidance (0 "runs through" errors, was 20).
2. Per-side pin classes (TOP/BOTTOM/LEFT/RIGHT, chosen by comparing box positions — the same arithmetic the built-in router's `routeEdge` already used) replaced a single shared center pin, which had been forcing every edge into one box to enter from the same side.
3. 3 pins per side instead of 1 (`SPREAD`), because one pin per side still bottlenecked every edge sharing a side into one corridor, which could run flush along a neighboring box's border.
4. `straightenEnd()` — a polyline post-processor, not a router setting. libavoid's own tuning (anglePenalty swept 200→20000, two nudge `RoutingOption`s) made zero difference to "does the last segment enter straight," because both path shapes cost the router the same number of bends. The fix edits the returned points: if the segment touching a pin runs *along* the border instead of *into* it, insert a short perpendicular stub so the bend moves one step earlier.
5. Card margin, label separation, forced-straight-entry, label wrapping — the four things Eryk asked for by name, all systemic (constants + checker rules, not spot patches).
6. Two real bugs found and fixed while doing #5: `declutter()` was packing the y-axis using a label's *width* not its *height*; the band-snap safety check excluded an edge's own endpoint boxes from its own collision check, so a label could land on its own source/target box undetected.
